name: The song of an Eurasian Wren
description:
Description
A Eurasian wren delivers an energetic and surprisingly powerful song from deep within dense vegetation. Rapid bursts of bright, ringing notes cascade into sharp trills and bubbling phrases, filling the surrounding space despite the bird’s tiny size. The song is lively and persistent, often repeated from concealed perches among shrubs, fallen branches, or ivy-covered woodland edges. Soft environmental ambience such as rustling leaves, distant birds, or faint wind movement creates a natural backdrop while the wren’s voice cuts clearly through the soundscape.

Meso
The wren occupies a focused central position in the acoustic scene, projecting a fast and complex sequence of notes that seem much larger than the bird itself. The surrounding habitat feels enclosed and textured, with vegetation subtly absorbing and reflecting the sound. Brief pauses separate intense vocal bursts, creating a rhythmic pattern within the quieter woodland ambience. Nearby environmental sounds remain subdued, emphasizing the sharp clarity and remarkable volume of the wren’s song.

Micro
Fine sonic details reveal rapid note modulation, metallic trills, crisp chirps, and abrupt tonal changes packed tightly together in short sequences. The song often accelerates into dense, sparkling phrases before ending suddenly in silence. Tiny echoes from nearby branches and foliage add depth and intimacy to the recording. Subtle background textures such as leaf movement, distant insects, or faint atmospheric noise contribute to the realism of the environment while preserving the prominence of the wren’s highly detailed vocal performance.

name: Winter forest NL 1108AM 220124_0326.flac
description: Quiet wintry forest in the Netherlands. There is hardly any wind. It's just after eleven in the morning. A great spotted woodpecker hammers some food from under the tree bark. A dog barks in the distance. People also come to this area to walk, but they are at a reasonable distance. Sometimes you hear there voices in the distance. The Short-Toed Treecreeper with her very high-pitched vocals. The great tit that sings very carefully that spring is coming, but that is only very occasionally. He doubts, as do I. It is still too cold and the days are short. Carrion Crows sometimes call. Suddenly two Great Spotted woodpeckers start a conversation. Or are these the first signs that they need to claim their territory? I don't know, I'm not an ornithologist. A Eurasian Wren keeps flying close to the microphones. You hear the rapid wing beat. After fifteen minutes, he starts yelling loudly nearby and at the microphones. His friend had started a little earlier, but at a further distance. There are always those careful scary brothers. When the brutal wren notices that the microphones are not responding at all and are therefore not dangerous, he leaves the battlefield resigned. The Wren flit about some more, the Carrion Crows finish my sound shooting, and I go home. Until next time. Moor frog’s and birds early March. Wind some (prop)planes. Fens and heathlands Kampina in the Netherlands spring day in March. This is the earliest sighting of moor frogs I have ever made. Around the water are patches of brownish grass and low shrubs. In the distance, a few more trees stand scattered across the gently rolling terrain. Typical view of the Zandbergsvennen in the Kampina nature reserve.

About the history of the Gelderse Waarden Polder, the Dutch fighting the waters and creating (new) nature for the future The Gelderse Waarden were created as a result of the dynamics of the River Meuse. Until the 15th century, the Meuse made a sharp bend between Well in the province Gelderland and Hedikhuizen in Brabant. This meander, known as the Hedikhuizense Maas, formed a natural border and was of great importance for local water management and shipping. In the winter of 1474-1475, this bend was dug through to facilitate shipping and limit flooding. This shifted the main flow of the Meuse to the north, placing the Gelderland lands south of the Meuse. After this intervention, the old Meuse arm gradually began to silt up. The Hedikhuizense Meuse changed from a wide river into a long, narrow waterway, partly even a ditch. The Hoge Maasdijk (on the left in the photo, where the trees are), which protects the area from high water, became an essential part of the landscape. Until 1958, the Gelderse Waarden belonged to the province of Gelderland. This made the area a U-shaped enclave of Gelderland in North Brabant. As part of the border corrections of 1958, the Gelderse Waarden were transferred to the province of North Brabant and the municipality of Heusden. From the year 1000 onwards, dykes were constructed to protect the land from flooding. The Hoge Maasdijk and the dyke along the old Meuse arm formed a closed dyke ring around the Land van Heusden en Altena. In the 18th and 19th centuries, spillways such as the Bokhoven and Baardwijk spillways were constructed to allow controlled flooding during extreme high water levels, thereby reducing the pressure on the dykes. The construction of the Bergsche Maas in 1904 and the Drongelens Canal in the same period marked the end of the natural flood dynamics. The river was canalised, weirs and groynes were constructed, and the landscape took on its current form. The Gelderse Waarden are part of the river area and contain valuable remnants of the former polder and river landscape. The area includes open water, marshes, wet hay meadows, copses and a dense network of ditches and trenches. The ecological value of the area is enhanced by the presence of wet nature reserves, such as De Sompen and Zooislagen, and its location near Natura 2000 protected nature. The area provides habitat for marsh birds, amphibians, bats and numerous insect and plant species. Various nature restoration projects are being carried out in the surrounding river area, aimed at restoring wet nature, improving water quality and increasing biodiversity. The Hoge Maasdijk (high water dike) protects the Gelderse Waarden against flooding from the Meuse. The dyke body is part of the regional flood defence system. The dyke has been reinforced in the past and adapted to the latest safety standards. The inundation system, with the inundation sluice at Fort Hedikhuizen, made it possible to let water in in a controlled manner when there was a threat, thereby inundating the hinterland to defend the fortress of Heusden. This system is of great historical importance and forms a cultural-historical element in the landscape. So you can see that we in the Netherlands are very busy with water management and nature development.

About the history of Holladay-park Vebenabos The history of the Vebenabos is directly linked to the reconstruction of Walcheren after the Second World War. During the war, Walcheren was flooded by the Allies in order to break through the German defences. After the liberation, large parts of the island had to be restored and replanted. This was carried out under the auspices of the ‘Nieuw Walcheren’ foundation. In June 1947, this foundation received a substantial donation for the reforestation of Walcheren from the directors of the Association for the Promotion of the Dutch Potato Trade (V.B.N.A.) — an association of potato farmers and traders from Groningen. At the time, a local spokesperson could say little more about it than that the woodland had been established by the potato farmers from Groningen. With this donation, a recreational area was created on the higher ground behind the dunes near Dishoek, which was initially called the V.B.N.A. Wood. Later, this name changed to ‘Vebena Wood’ and eventually to ‘Vebenabos’. In 1949, one of Zeeland’s first holiday parks was built in the Vebenabos near Dishoek, and it still exudes the atmosphere of living in the woods. This was part of the wider development of Dishoek as a recreational area, which had already begun to flourish slowly after the First World War with cycle paths, beach stalls and the first guesthouse (1930), which later became the Westduin Hotel. The site is owned by the Vebenabos Foundation, whilst the owners of the holiday homes are members of the Vebenabos Holiday Home Owners’ Association (VEZV). From 1966 to 1997, Vebenabos belonged to the municipality of Valkenisse, and was subsequently incorporated into the municipality of Veere. Prior to that, until 1 July 1966, the area fell under the municipality of Koudekerke. Dishoek itself is much older: the hamlet originated around 1293 as a dyke, from which it takes its name — a corruption of ‘Dyckshoecke’, the spot where the young dunes merged with the dyke leading towards Vlissingen. name: village fields Cromvoirt Netherlands 1035 AM 241103_0937
description: Quiet autumn Sunday morning in the fields at stream De Zandleij in Cromvoirt, North Brabant, Netherlands. Behind me is a farm with geese. Cows graze on the right and in the distance electric trains run at high speed from town to town. In the trees and bushes along the water are many very small birds like the Great Tit and the Wren. Crows, Jackdaws and Jays can always be heard here. Occasionally a group of tough men on mountain bikes ride down the dirt road. About the stream Zandleij The Zandleij is a watercourse in the Dutch province of North Brabant. It starts north of Tilburg. From here the river flowed in a northeasterly direction, through the wet and low-lying nature reserve De Brand north of Udenhout, and then past Zwijnsbergen Castle near Helvoirt. The current then bends in a northerly direction and cuts through the cover sand ridge. At Cromvoirt the Zandleij ends in the 's-Hertogenbosch-Drongelen drainage canal. The Zand-leij stream has never been completely natural, the name of which is 'leij', which means 'to guide'. It is assumed that the Zandleij was dug between the 14th and 18th centuries. In the 1960s there were capacity problems and a new bed was dug. The original bed is now called Zandkantse Leij. Water quality This water is different from natural water and far from clean. On this page we tell you more about the quality of the water from the Zandleij and why it is better to avoid contact with this water, for humans and animals. The Zandleij is a stream with a length of about 13 kilometers. It starts in Tilburg North and flows through Udenhout, Helvoirt and Cromvoirt to end in the Drongelens Kanaal near Vught. From our sewage plants, purified wastewater flows into the stream. Usually it ends up in an existing stream through which water already flows. For the Zandleij the purified wastewater is the main source, supplemented with rainwater in wet periods. In dry months, almost only treated wastewater flows through the Zandleij. About the village of Cromvoirt The name Cromvoirt consists of the parts crom and voirt. This combination of words means; wet land that can be walked through. The settlement of Cromvoirt must have originated around 1100 at the transition between higher sandy soils and the low-lying river valley of the Meuse. The low-lying village of Cromvoirt is located between two higher parts: the Vughterheide in the east and the De Loonse en Drunense Duinen National Park in the west. About the stream Zandleij where I am The Zandleij is a watercourse in the Dutch province of North Brabant. It starts north of Tilburg. From here the river flowed in a northeasterly direction, through the wet and low-lying nature reserve De Brand north of Udenhout, and then past Zwijnsbergen Castle near Helvoirt. The current then bends in a northerly direction and cuts through the cover sand ridge. At Cromvoirt the Zandleij ends in the 's-Hertogenbosch-Drongelen drainage canal. The Zand-leij stream has never been completely natural, the name of which is 'leij', which means 'to guide'. It is assumed that the Zandleij was dug between the 14th and 18th centuries. In the 1960s there were capacity problems and a new bed was dug. The original bed is now called Zandkantse Leij. The canal collects seepage water and thus contributes to the desiccation of the De Brand nature reserve, while during excessive rainfall this area is flooded with polluted water from elsewhere. About the village of Cromvoirt The name Cromvoirt consists of the parts crom and voirt. This combination of words means; wet land that can be walked through. The settlement of Cromvoirt must have originated around 1100 at the transition between higher sandy soils and the low-lying river valley of the Meuse. The low-lying village of Cromvoirt is located between two higher parts: the Vughterheide in the east and the De Loonse en Drunense Duinen National Park in the west. About the history of Holladay-park Vebenabos The history of the Vebenabos is directly linked to the reconstruction of Walcheren after the Second World War. During the war, Walcheren was flooded by the Allies in order to break through the German defences. After the liberation, large parts of the island had to be restored and replanted. This was carried out under the auspices of the ‘Nieuw Walcheren’ foundation. In June 1947, this foundation received a substantial donation for the reforestation of Walcheren from the directors of the Association for the Promotion of the Dutch Potato Trade (V.B.N.A.) — an association of potato farmers and traders from Groningen. At the time, a local spokesperson could say little more about it than that the woodland had been established by the potato farmers from Groningen. With this donation, a recreational area was created on the higher ground behind the dunes near Dishoek, which was initially called the V.B.N.A. Wood. Later, this name changed to ‘Vebena Wood’ and eventually to ‘Vebenabos’. In 1949, one of Zeeland’s first holiday parks was built in the Vebenabos near Dishoek, and it still exudes the atmosphere of living in the woods. This was part of the wider development of Dishoek as a recreational area, which had already begun to flourish slowly after the First World War with cycle paths, beach stalls and the first guesthouse (1930), which later became the Westduin Hotel. The site is owned by the Vebenabos Foundation, whilst the owners of the holiday homes are members of the Vebenabos Holiday Home Owners’ Association (VEZV). From 1966 to 1997, Vebenabos belonged to the municipality of Valkenisse, and was subsequently incorporated into the municipality of Veere. Prior to that, until 1 July 1966, the area fell under the municipality of Koudekerke. Dishoek itself is much older: the hamlet originated around 1293 as a dyke, from which it takes its name — a corruption of ‘Dyckshoecke’, the spot where the young dunes merged with the dyke leading towards Vlissingen. The area therefore has a long history of dyke construction and coastal protection, long before the forest was established there.

name: Female alligator bellow and juveniles answer, SMNWR
description: Three minutes of early morning female mother alligator vocalization with her juvenile alligators in a shallow primarily freshwater depression type pond near Ring Dike and Cedar Creek east of Stoney Bayou Pool in the St Marks National Wildlife Refuge. May 2023. Sony PCM M10 recorder, Clippy EM272Z1 stereo microphones, windbubbles & drybags. One way I differentiate between male and female adult alligator bellows, besides seeing the alligator, is through spectrogram analysis.  Male bellows tend to have more infrasound (usually 16 to 20Hz) components to their bellow than females.  I know this gator was a mother because of her interactions with the hatchlings. Carolina wren and Eastern Wood-Pewee calls can be heard in the background as well as Southern Cricket frogs and Green Tree Frogs.

name: CarolinaWrenCallJanuary2014.mp3
description:
This Carolina Wren was braving a very cold, gusting cold front in early January. Recording made in a small midwestern town using my Zoom H4-N recorder and its own internal microphones set at a record volume of 80.

**Note that since there were some strong north winds, you will hear the wind/roar in the background, but this Wren just seemed oblivious to it.
